e.etymology: A K spelling of Callie, a pet form of Caroline and of names beginning with Cal- such as Calista and Calliope, which draw on Greek kallos, beauty.
From Arabic inaya, care or concern, often understood as God's care. It is used by Muslim families in South Asia and the West, alongside the related Inayat.
Several names share this form: Albanian Zamir, from ze, voice, and mire, good; Hebrew zamir, song or nightingale; and Arabic damir, conscience, pronounced zamir in Urdu and Persian.

e.meaning: from Brittany, land of the Britons
e.etymology: From Brittany, the region of northwest France named for the Britons who settled it. It was first used as a given name in the US in the 1970s and peaked around 1990.
namesakes: Brittany Murphy (actress in Clueless and 8 Mile)

assoc.t: pop star Britney Spears, who spells it Britney
Brittany, the region of northwest France
Brittany, a breed of bird-hunting spaniel

e.note: Reads as a name of the late 1980s and early 90s, when it was a US top-ten girls' name.

e.meaning: of the family of Julius; traditionally youthful
e.etymology: The Italian form of Juliana, from Latin Iuliana, the feminine of Iulianus, of the family of Julius. It is often also heard as a blend of Giulia and Anna.
e.note: The Italian Giu- spelling is often miswritten Guiliana in the US.

e.etymology: The anglicized form of Irish Niall, a name of disputed origin, most often explained as champion or cloud. Niall of the Nine Hostages was a legendary Irish high king.
namesakes: Neil Armstrong (first person to walk on the moon)

assoc.t: Neil Armstrong, first person to walk on the moon

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yehudit, woman of Judea, the feminine of Judah. The heroine of the Book of Judith saves her city by beheading the general Holofernes.
A Spanish phonetic spelling of the Irish name Brian, usually linked to a Celtic root for high or noble. It is widespread in Latin America and among US Latino families.
e.note: In Colombia and parts of Latin America, Brayan carries a stereotype of a reckless young man.

e.etymology: From the South Slavic word zora, dawn. In the US it is best known through the writer Zora Neale Hurston.
namesakes: Zora Neale Hurston (author of Their Eyes Were Watching God)

assoc.t: the Zora, an aquatic people in The Legend of Zelda games

e.etymology: A modern Indian name, popular with Hindu families since the 2010s and usually explained as free of flaws; its Sanskrit derivation is not settled.
From Spanish luz, light, shortened from María de la Luz, a title of the Virgin Mary as Our Lady of Light.
e.note: English speakers often say it like the word lose or loose.

e.etymology: A Spanish-style phonetic spelling in the Kayla and Keila family, favored by Latino families. Kayla began as a short form of Michaela; Keila is also the name of a town in the Hebrew Bible.
From Spanish cielo, sky or heaven, from Latin caelum; mi cielo is also a Spanish term of endearment.
From the English county of Devon, Old English Defenas, the Devonians, a name going back to the Celtic Dumnonii. It is also treated as a variant of Devin.
namesakes: Devon Sawa (actor in Casper and Final Destination)

assoc.t: Devon, a county in southwest England

e.etymology: Of uncertain origin; in use in the US by the 1880s, possibly as a variant of Veda or a short form of Nevada. Vada Sultenfuss is the heroine of the 1991 film My Girl.
namesakes: Vada Sultenfuss (Anna Chlumsky's character in My Girl)

assoc.t: vada, a savory fried snack in South Indian cooking

e.etymology: Appears in the King James Bible as a form of Isshiah, a minor Old Testament name. Today it is mostly chosen as a variation on Josiah with the sound of Jesse.
From the Hebrew word shai, gift. In the US it is also used as a spelling of Shay, and has risen with NBA star Shai Gilgeous-Alexander.
namesakes: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander (NBA MVP guard for the Oklahoma City Thunder)

assoc.t: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, NBA star and 2025 MVP

e.etymology: A modern American name in the family of Alaia, Alayah and Aaliyah. Alaia is linked to a Basque word for joyful and to the fashion house Alaïa.
An English surname, an alteration of Nickson, son of Nick, the short form of Nicholas. It joined the run of x-names such as Jaxon and Paxton in the 2010s.

assoc.t: Richard Nixon, president who resigned over Watergate
Nixon, watch and accessories brand

e.note: Most Americans hear President Richard Nixon and the Watergate scandal first.

e.etymology: A surname with several sources: Low German from the personal name Bode, messenger; Irish Ó Buadáin; and an English variant of Bawden. As a first name it sits beside Bowen and Bodhi.

assoc.t: Boden, British clothing retailer known for kids' wear

e.etymology: Derived from the Shona name Tendai, give thanks. The actress Zendaya Coleman was given this form by her parents, and nearly all American use follows her.
namesakes: Zendaya (actress in Euphoria, Dune and Spider-Man)

assoc.t: Zendaya, actress and singer known by the one name

e.etymology: A respelling of Aileen, the Scottish form of Eileen, which anglicizes the Irish Eibhlín, itself from the Norman French Aveline. The Turkish name Aylin sounds much the same.
A respelling of Kalani, from Hawaiian ka lani, the sky or the heavens, a word also used of chiefs. One of several spellings that rose in the late 2010s beside Kehlani and Kailani.
The toad-riding ninja hero of a 19th-century Japanese tale, his name written with characters read as young thunder. American use comes from the character Jiraiya in the anime Naruto.

assoc.t: Jiraiya, Naruto's mentor in the anime Naruto

e.note: In Naruto the character is a beloved mentor but also a comic lecher nicknamed the Pervy Sage.

e.etymology: A Scottish surname from Gaelic buidhe, yellow or fair-haired, and an Irish one from Ó Buadhaigh, descendant of the victorious. As a first name it honors David Bowie.
namesakes: Jim Bowie (frontiersman who died at the Alamo)

assoc.t: David Bowie, rock star who created Ziggy Stardust
Bowie knife, large American hunting and fighting knife

e.etymology: A German and Swedish short form of Margareta, from Greek margarites, pearl. It is recorded in Sweden as early as 1309.

assoc.t: Greta Thunberg, Swedish climate activist known as Greta
Greta Garbo, classic Hollywood star

e.etymology: From Greek Kynthia, of Mount Cynthus on the island of Delos, a title of Artemis, who was said to be born there. Poets used it for the moon, and it became an English given name in the 17th century.
namesakes: Cynthia Erivo (actress and singer in Wicked)
Cynthia Nixon (Sex and the City actress)

assoc.t: Cynthia, Angelica's doll in Rugrats

e.etymology: A Japanese name whose meaning depends on the characters chosen; kai is often written as sea. American use took off with Kairi, the heroine of the Kingdom Hearts games. Estonian has an unrelated Kairi.

assoc.t: Kairi, heroine of the Kingdom Hearts video games

e.etymology: A variant of Quentin, from the Roman name Quintinus, from Latin quintus, fifth, merged with an English surname from a place name meaning queen's town.
namesakes: Quinton Jackson (mixed martial artist known as Rampage)

e.etymology: A modern American coinage, said like Drew with a J. It became a baby name through NBA guard Jrue Holiday.

assoc.t: Jrue Holiday, NBA champion guard

e.note: Sounds like Drew, so it is often misheard and misspelled.

e.meaning: a fragrant flowering plant; also read as father's adornment
e.etymology: From Arabic Zaynab, the name of a fragrant desert plant, also explained as zayn, beauty, plus ab, father. A daughter and a granddaughter of the Prophet Muhammad bore the name.
In India usually taken from Sanskrit ayana, a path or the sun's course. Muslim families in South Asia also use it, often explained as gift of God, though that Arabic derivation is uncertain.
